solution.overview: A strong answer sorts the eight balances by their normal side: debit balances are customers (accounts receivable) and credit balances are vendors (accounts payable). It presents a schedule of accounts receivable totaling $2,490 and a schedule of accounts payable totaling $3,995, explains that each total must agree with its controlling account in the general ledger, and ties the discussion to special journals and subsidiary ledgers.

answer: Accounts receivable is an asset with a normal debit balance, so every debit-balance name is a customer who owes Piper's Pets
Freddie Perkins $710, Furry Friends $85, Paul Ryan $95, Pets R Us $1,350, Sally Sue $250
Total accounts receivable = $2,490
This total must equal the Accounts Receivable controlling account in the general ledger
Accounts payable is a liability with a normal credit balance, so every credit-balance name is a vendor Piper's Pets owes
Kitty Litters $1,245, Lions, Tigers, and Bears Oh My $630, Office Super Store $2,120
Total accounts payable = $3,995
This total must equal the Accounts Payable controlling account in the general ledger

by_task.task: Nature of accounts receivable and accounts payable
answer: Accounts receivable: amounts customers owe the business for sales on account; a current asset that will become cash when collected
Accounts payable: amounts the business owes vendors for purchases on account; a current liability that must be paid, usually within 30 to 60 days
Both are tracked customer by customer or vendor by vendor in subsidiary ledgers, and the schedules prove those ledgers agree with the general ledger
Special journals record one type of frequent transaction each: sales journal (sales on account), purchases journal (purchases on account), cash receipts journal and cash payments journal
They save time because column totals are posted to the general ledger once a period, while individual amounts post daily to the subsidiary ledgers
The general journal is still used for transactions that do not fit a special journal, such as adjusting and closing entries

judge_question_answers.question: If a business only has 2 or 3 vendors do you think it is necessary to prepare a schedule?
answer: Yes, a schedule is still good practice even if it is short
It proves that the subsidiary ledger agrees with the controlling account and documents exactly who is owed how much at year end
It takes little time with few vendors and builds a habit that scales as the business grows

judge_question_answers.question: Are any GAAP principals ignored when a company does not use subsidiary ledgers?
answer: No specific GAAP principle requires subsidiary ledgers; they are a bookkeeping control, not a reporting rule
Without them, though, it is harder to support the accuracy and full disclosure of the receivable and payable balances reported on the balance sheet
Good internal control and the objective evidence concept are better served when detailed records back up the controlling accounts

judge_question_answers.question: What procedure would you recommend be established for extending credit to individuals or companies?
answer: Require a credit application and check credit references or a credit report before approving
Set a credit limit and clear payment terms (for example net 30) for each customer
Review an aging of accounts receivable regularly and stop extending credit to slow payers

key_concepts.definition: Money customers owe the business for goods or services sold on account. It is a current asset with a normal debit balance.
Money the business owes vendors for goods or services bought on account. It is a current liability with a normal credit balance.
A list of every customer's balance from the AR subsidiary ledger. Its total must equal the Accounts Receivable controlling account in the general ledger.
A list of every vendor's balance from the AP subsidiary ledger. Its total must equal the Accounts Payable controlling account in the general ledger.
A ledger that holds the detailed accounts (one per customer or vendor) that together make up a single controlling account in the general ledger.
A general ledger account (such as Accounts Receivable or Accounts Payable) whose balance equals the total of all accounts in its subsidiary ledger.
Journals used for one type of frequent transaction: sales journal, purchases journal, cash receipts journal and cash payments journal. Column totals are posted to the general ledger at period end.
The side (debit or credit) on which an account increases. Assets and expenses have debit normal balances; liabilities, equity and revenue have credit normal balances.
The rules a business uses before selling on account: credit application, reference checks, credit limits and payment terms, plus regular aging reviews.

roleplays.title: ABC Manufacturing: cash control training, bank reconciliation, petty cash and service charge entries
roleplays.participant_role: Controller (head accountant) for ABC Manufacturing training a newly hired accountant
roleplays.judge_role: Newly hired accountant for ABC Manufacturing who will take over cash control duties
roleplays.scenario:
You are to assume the role of controller (head accountant) for ABC manufacturing. You have just hired an accountant (judge) to handle some of your duties, including controlling the cash account. Your job is to train the new accountant (judge) on how to perform basic cash control procedures.

According to your records, the company has the following:

Balance of cash in Checkbook (stub 134): $14,300
Total Outstanding Checks: $2,000
Total Outstanding Deposits: $4,000
Service Charge: $50
Balance of cash on Bank Statement (12/31/13): $12,250

Demonstrate to the new accountant (judge) how to reconcile a bank account in order to prove cash. In addition to explaining all necessary cash control procedures and the benefits of EFT, you should demonstrate to the new accountant (judge) how to journalize establishment of petty cash fund of $200 and bank service charge entries.

You will conduct your training in the new accountant's (judge's) office. The new accountant (judge) will begin the role play by greeting you as you enter his/her office. You will proceed to provide training in cash control systems. After you have conducted your training and answered the new accountant's (judge's) questions, the new accountant (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your help.
tasks: Demonstrate to the new accountant (judge) how to reconcile a bank account in order to prove cash
Explain all necessary cash control procedures
Explain the benefits of EFT
Demonstrate how to journalize establishment of petty cash fund of $200
Demonstrate how to journalize bank service charge entries

solution.overview: A strong answer walks the new accountant through a two-column bank reconciliation that proves cash at $14,250 on both sides, explains why cash needs controls because it is the most liquid asset, lists specific procedures, journalizes the $200 petty cash fund and the $50 service charge, and closes with the time and cost benefits of EFT.

answer: Cash is the most liquid asset, so it is the easiest to lose or steal and needs formal procedures
Reconcile the bank account every month
Use restrictive endorsements on checks received ("For deposit only")
Keep signature cards on file and require check approval before signing
Deposit cash promptly and establish a petty cash fund for small purchases
Start with the checkbook balance of $14,300 and deduct the $50 service charge: adjusted checkbook balance $14,250
Start with the bank statement balance of $12,250, add outstanding deposits of $4,000 and subtract outstanding checks of $2,000: adjusted bank balance $14,250
Both adjusted balances equal $14,250, so cash is proved
Even a difference of a few cents must be investigated because it may be the tip of a larger problem
Debit Petty Cash $200 and credit Cash $200
Petty cash lets the business pay for small, immaterial items without writing a check
Debit Miscellaneous Expense $50 and credit Cash $50
This entry brings the checkbook balance down to the adjusted balance of $14,250
Saves time because no checks have to be written
Reduces the lag between paying and the payment clearing the bank
Cuts postage and check printing fees

journal_entries.description: Record bank service charge
Establish petty cash fund

calculations.label: Bank reconciliation, bank side
calculations.result: $14,250 (matches adjusted checkbook balance, cash is proved)

judge_question_answers.question: Does it really matter if the bank reconciliation is only off a few cents?
answer: Yes, even a small difference could be the tip of the iceberg
A few cents may point to a much larger error or a control problem that must be found

judge_question_answers.question: What is the need for a petty cash account?
answer: Petty cash is used for small transactions
It lets the business avoid writing a check for immaterial purchases

judge_question_answers.question: How do you determine if a check is outstanding?
answer: A check is outstanding if it has been written but has not yet cleared the bank
Start with the checkbook and compare it to the bank statement to see which checks cleared and which did not

key_concepts.definition: A schedule that explains the difference between the checkbook balance and the bank statement balance. Adjusted checkbook balance (checkbook balance minus service charges and other bank deductions) must equal adjusted bank balance (bank balance plus outstanding deposits minus outstanding checks).
Showing that the cash recorded in the books agrees with the actual cash in the bank after reconciling items are considered.
A check the business has written and recorded but that has not yet cleared the bank, so it is subtracted from the bank statement balance.
A deposit the business has recorded that the bank has not yet added to the statement, so it is added to the bank statement balance.
A fee the bank deducts from the account. It is recorded with a debit to Miscellaneous Expense and a credit to Cash after the reconciliation reveals it.
A small amount of cash kept on hand to pay for minor expenses. Establishing it is recorded as a debit to Petty Cash and a credit to Cash.
Internal controls that protect cash because it is so liquid: monthly bank reconciliations, restrictive endorsements, signature cards, check approval, prompt deposits and a petty cash fund.
Writing "For deposit only" on the back of a received check so it can only be deposited into the company account and not cashed by someone else.
Moving money between bank accounts electronically instead of by paper check, which saves time, shortens clearing delays and reduces postage and check costs.

roleplays.title: Timber Valley Landscaping: equipment purchase on credit, income statement effect and accounting equation
roleplays.participant_role: CPA advising the owner of Timber Valley Landscaping on an equipment purchase
roleplays.judge_role: Owner of Timber Valley Landscaping deciding whether to buy a new piece of equipment on credit
roleplays.scenario:
You are to assume the role of a CPA for Timber Valley Landscaping. The owner (judge) is trying to decide if she should purchase a new piece of equipment. She has asked you for advice so she can make a financially sound business decision.

The new piece of equipment will cost $50,000 and will last 5 years. The owner has indicated that the equipment will allow the business to generate $50,000 more in sales each year. The Owner (judge) wants to purchase the equipment on credit. Show how adding the new equipment will affect Timber Valley's Income Statement and Owner's Equity for the next two years. Break down the purchase of $50,000 of equipment on credit into debits and credits using a general journal that you create. Explain to the owner how the purchase of equipment will affect the accounting equation and ultimately the Balance Sheet.

You will present your recommendation to the owner (judge) in a role-play that will take place in the owner's office. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented your recommendation and have answered the owner's (judge's) question, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.
tasks: Show how adding the new equipment will affect Timber Valley's Income Statement and Owner's Equity for the next two years
Break down the purchase of $50,000 of equipment on credit into debits and credits using a general journal that you create
Explain to the owner how the purchase of equipment will affect the accounting equation and ultimately the Balance Sheet

solution.overview: A strong answer shows that the equipment adds $50,000 of sales and $10,000 of straight-line depreciation each year, so net income and owner's equity rise by $40,000 in each of the next two years. It records the credit purchase as a debit to Equipment and a credit to Accounts Payable, shows that assets and liabilities both rise by $50,000 so A = L + OE stays balanced, and explains accounts payable, the accounting cycle and the advisory role of a CPA.

by_task.task: Income statement and owner's equity effect (two years)
answer: Annual depreciation = $50,000 cost / 5 years = $10,000 per year
Year 1: sales $50,000 minus depreciation $10,000 = net income $40,000
Year 2: same, sales $50,000 minus depreciation $10,000 = net income $40,000
Net income flows into owner's equity, so equity increases by $40,000 each year ($80,000 over two years)
Recommend the purchase because the added income far exceeds the yearly cost of the equipment

by_task.task: General journal entry for the credit purchase
answer: Create a journal with at least account titles and debit and credit columns (date, source document and posting reference columns are optional extras)
Debit Equipment $50,000
Credit Accounts Payable (or another liability) $50,000

by_task.task: Accounting equation and balance sheet effect
answer: Assets increase by $50,000 (Equipment) and liabilities increase by $50,000 (Accounts Payable)
Because both sides rise by the same amount, Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity stays in balance
Owner's equity is not changed by the purchase itself, only by the income the equipment later earns
Accounts payable is a liability, an "IOU" to the vendor
The business owes the money now and must repay it in the future

by_task.task: Role of a CPA and the accounting cycle
answer: A CPA advises the owner on how business decisions affect the company's financial position; the final decision stays with the owner
Accounting cycle: analyze transactions, journalize, post to the ledger, prepare a worksheet, prepare financial statements, record adjusting and closing entries, prepare a post-closing trial balance
The cycle repeats monthly and yearly so management gets timely financial information, and every transaction ends up in the financial statements

calculations.label: Annual depreciation (straight-line)
steps: $50,000 cost / 5 year useful life = $10,000 per year

calculations.label: Income statement effect, Year 1 (and Year 2)
calculations.result: Net income increases $40,000 each year; owner's equity increases $40,000 each year

judge_question_answers.question: If the equipment were purchased for cash (instead of a loan), how would this affect the accounting equation?
answer: Equipment (an asset) increases by $50,000 and Cash (an asset) decreases by $50,000
Net effect on total assets is $0
No effect on liabilities or owner's equity

judge_question_answers.question: How would a useful life of 10 years for the equipment affect the decision?
answer: It would make the purchase more attractive
The $50,000 cost would be spread over 10 years instead of 5, so depreciation drops to $5,000 per year and net income rises to $45,000 per year

judge_question_answers.question: How does an increase in income affect Owner's Equity?
answer: Increases in income increase owner's equity
Net income is closed into the owner's capital account at the end of the period

key_concepts.definition: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity. Every transaction keeps the two sides equal.

The repeating steps of accounting: analyze transactions, journalize, post to the ledger, prepare a worksheet, prepare financial statements, record adjusting and closing entries, and prepare a post-closing trial balance.
The book of original entry where each transaction is recorded with the date, account titles, and debit and credit amounts (debits listed first).
A liability representing money the business owes to vendors for purchases made on credit, an "IOU" that must be paid in the future.
Spreading the cost of a long-lived asset evenly over its useful life. Annual depreciation = (cost minus salvage value) / useful life; here $50,000 / 5 = $10,000 per year.
Revenues minus expenses for a period. Net income increases owner's equity; a net loss decreases it.
The owner's claim on the assets of the business (assets minus liabilities). It rises with owner investments and net income and falls with withdrawals and net losses.
Buying an asset now and paying later. Assets and liabilities both increase by the same amount, so the accounting equation stays balanced.
A certified public accountant advises business owners on the financial effects of decisions, but the decision itself belongs to the owner or manager.

roleplays.title: Rocking Ribs restaurant: low-season staffing, fixed vs. variable costs and cost-volume-profit
roleplays.participant_role: Experienced restaurant owner of Rocking Ribs explaining low-season cost decisions to a partner
roleplays.judge_role: Partner who invested startup funds in Rocking Ribs but knows little about restaurant operations or cost accounting
roleplays.scenario:
You are to assume the role of a restaurant owner in a beachside location called, ROCKING RIBS. Your partner (judge) has invested startup funds for ROCKING RIBS but knows very little about the daily operations of running a restaurant or cost accounting.

Since your restaurant is just across the street from the beach in a tourist area, your sales greatly fluctuate from high season to low season. Your 50 table restaurant is known for its tender meat, which cooks over low flames for 14 hours. You must make sure you order and cook enough meat the night before because if you run out of an item, you cannot just pull it from the freezer and cook it on the spot.

During high season
- ROCKING RIBS fills to capacity.
- ROCKING RIBS is open 12 hours a day 7 days a week. (totaling 336 hours a month)
- ROCKING RIBS employs 8 servers and 3 cooks.
- Servers are paid $5 per hour plus tips, cooks earn $10 per hour.
- To staff the restaurant for the month, it costs $23,520.
- The fixed cost of rent, insurance and utilities is $4,300.
- The monthly meat order costs $80,000.
- The mark up on meat is 1 1/2 times what it costs. This makes sales in high season average $120,000.
- ROCKING RIBS maintains a profit margin of just about 10%

During low season about half of your customers return to their summer homes so you only order half as much meat.

[Table: High season vs. Low season costs, see exhibits]

[Table: Staffing cost per employee, see exhibits]

Now that high season has ended and low season is starting, your partner (judge) has asked you to explain how you determine the following for low season:
- Appropriate number of employees using data mining
- Potential risks of overscheduling employees
- Potential risks of food surplus
- Fixed vs. Variable costs

You will present your expertise to your partner (judge) in a role-play to take place in your office. Your partner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear about low season. After you have presented your explanation and have answered your partner's (judge's) questions, your partner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your advice.

solution.overview: A strong answer separates fixed costs (rent, insurance, utilities of $4,300) from variable costs (food and payroll), works backward from low-season sales of $60,000 and a 10% profit target to show that only $9,700 is available for salaries, and uses the staffing table to show which server and cook combinations fit that budget. It then explains the risks of overscheduling and food surplus, the purpose of cost accounting and CVP analysis, and other factors that affect business risk.

answer: Fixed costs stay the same in total no matter the activity level; here they are rent, insurance and utilities, $4,300 per month in both seasons
Fixed cost per unit falls as volume rises and rises as volume falls
Variable costs change in total in direct proportion to activity but stay the same per unit; here they are food (meat) and payroll
Food drops from $80,000 to $40,000 in low season because half the customers leave

by_task.task: Low season salary budget and number of employees
answer: Low-season meat order = half of $80,000 = $40,000
Low-season sales = $40,000 x 1.5 markup = $60,000
Target profit = 10% x $60,000 = $6,000
Fixed costs $4,300 + meat $40,000 + profit $6,000 = $50,300; $60,000 minus $50,300 = $9,700 available for salaries

Using the staffing table, 3 servers ($5,040) plus 2 cooks ($6,720) = $11,760, which is over the $9,700 budget, so a smaller combination such as 3 servers and 1 cook ($5,040 + $3,360 = $8,400) or 2 servers and 1 cook ($3,360 + $3,360 = $6,720) fits
Data mining past sales data (when customers visit, what they order) helps predict demand so staffing and meat orders match actual traffic
Every extra employee hour is a variable cost that is not covered by low-season sales
Scheduling too many staff cuts profit below the 10% target or pushes the restaurant into the red
Example: 3 servers and 2 cooks cost $11,760, which exceeds the $9,700 salary budget by $2,060
Meat must be cooked 14 hours ahead, so anything ordered and cooked but not sold is wasted
Wasted meat is wasted money and directly reduces profit
Ordering too little is also a risk because you cannot cook more on the spot, so accurate forecasting matters

by_task.task: Cost accounting, CVP and business risk
answer: Managerial cost accounting prepares reports for internal users and measures the cost, profitability and performance of operations to support decisions
Cost accounting decision making uses total and unit cost data to decide what to offer, what price to charge and how much to produce
CVP analysis studies how changes in costs and volume affect profit; breakeven is where sales = variable costs + fixed costs
Other factors affecting business risk: target market and seasonal tourist counts, disposable income of residents, supply and demand, economic growth and competition

judge_question_answers.question: What other business opportunities might I consider to make the business more profitable during low season?
answer: Sell branded merchandise (t-shirts, souvenir glasses, beach gear) and bottled BBQ sauce, in store and shipped to out-of-town customers
Start a frozen dinner line with online ordering and shipping
Cater parties, rent the restaurant for school events and fundraisers, or run catering trucks at sporting events
Host an "in the biz" night for local hospitality workers, deliver to year-round neighborhoods, or consider relocating nearer year-round residents

judge_question_answers.question: What other ways could you decrease expenses to survive low season without running in the red?
answer: Lower utilities: seat guests only in the main dining area, turn off chillers in unused areas, run only one freezer and one deep fryer
Cut staff hours per week; letting employees go should be a last resort
Reduce the number of menu items so you do not have to stock everything offered in high season
Shorten hours of operation when the restaurant is not busy

key_concepts.definition: A cost that stays the same in total regardless of activity level, such as rent, insurance, property taxes and depreciation. Fixed cost per unit falls as volume rises.
A cost that changes in total in direct proportion to activity but stays constant per unit, such as food ingredients, direct labor and sales commissions.
Accounting done for internal users (managers) that measures, analyzes and reports the cost, profitability and performance of operations to support decisions.
Using total cost and unit cost information to decide which products to offer, what price to charge and how much to produce.
The study of how changes in costs and sales volume affect profit. It is used in profit planning and to find the breakeven point.
The level of sales where the business makes no profit and no loss: Sales = Variable costs + Fixed costs.
Profit as a percentage of sales: Profit margin = Net profit / Sales. Rocking Ribs targets about 10%.
The amount added to cost to set the selling price. Meat marked up 1.5 times cost means $40,000 of meat produces $60,000 of sales.

A rate used to assign indirect (overhead) costs to products or services: Overhead rate = Estimated overhead / Estimated activity base (such as labor hours). Here the $4,300 of fixed overhead spread over 336 open hours is about $12.80 per hour.
Analyzing stored data from many angles to find useful patterns, for example when customers visit and what they order, to plan staffing and food orders.
Factors that can hurt profit, such as seasonal target market changes, residents' disposable income, supply and demand, economic growth and competition.

answer: Accounting is a system of recording and summarizing business and financial transactions; it identifies, records and communicates relevant, reliable and comparable information to interested users
Business entity concept: the business is accounted for separately from its owner
Dual aspect concept: every transaction has two effects, which is why debits always equal credits
Going concern and accounting period concepts: the business is assumed to continue indefinitely, and its life is split into periods so statements can be prepared regularly
Cost and money measurement concepts: only transactions that can be expressed in money are recorded, at cost
Matching concept: expenses of a period, paid or not, are matched against the revenue they helped earn

by_task.task: Effects of transactions on the accounting equation
answer: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity (shareholders' equity for a corporation)
A company can pay for an asset with another asset (cash), with a liability (debt) or with owner's equity (investment or retained earnings)
Liabilities can be paid down with assets such as cash or by taking on new debt
Every transaction keeps the equation in balance, and the balance sheet shows this: $769,001 = $17,020 + $751,981
Example: buying DJ equipment on account raises Equipment (asset) and Accounts Payable (liability) by the same amount

by_task.task: Nature of the income statement (client's 2015 statement)
answer: An income statement shows financial performance over a period of time, here the year ended December 31, 2015
Operating revenue $540,253 is money earned from selling the company's services; cost of services sold $23,420 is what it cost to provide them, leaving gross profit of $516,833
Operating expenses $13,163 combine selling expenses ($1,995) and administrative expenses ($11,168) that are not directly tied to producing the service
Income from operations $503,670 = gross profit minus operating expenses; other revenue of $500 is bank interest earned outside normal operations
Net income before tax $504,170, less federal income tax $2,044, gives the bottom line net income of $502,126; units of services sold (1,285) shows volume for the period

by_task.task: Nature of the balance sheet (client's 2015 statement)

Assets $769,001 are resources the company owns with future economic value: cash $502,126, accounts receivable $1,875 and DJ equipment $265,000
Liabilities $17,020 are debts owed to others: two accounts payable ($6,275 and $10,245) and a $500 note payable
Owner's equity $751,981 is the owner's investment minus withdrawals plus net income since the business began
Total assets equal total liabilities plus owner's equity, proving the accounting equation

by_task.task: Nature of the cash flow statement
answer: Shows a company's gross cash receipts and gross cash payments for a period and tells a lot about liquidity
Operating activities: cash from day-to-day business
Investing activities: cash spent on capital expenditures and acquisitions
Financing activities: cash from borrowing or selling stock and cash used to repay loans or pay dividends

Each section nets cash in and cash out; the net increase in cash should be positive. A negative net change is a red flag that the company may not have enough cash to meet obligations and must be monitored closely

solution.overview: A strong answer is a clear training-style overview: it sorts business transactions into types (cash vs. credit, purchases, sales, receipts, payments, and internal vs. external), explains accounts receivable as a short-term asset owed by customers and accounts payable as a short-term liability owed to suppliers, defines accounting as recording, sorting and summarizing transactions into reports, and shows why accurate financial information matters to managers, owners, creditors and the tax authorities, especially for a fast-growing furniture manufacturer.

answer: Cash transactions are paid or received immediately; credit (on account) transactions are paid later and create receivables or payables
By activity: purchases of materials, sales of furniture, cash receipts from customers, cash payments to suppliers and employees
External transactions are with outside parties (customers, suppliers, lenders); internal transactions happen within the company (using up supplies, recording depreciation)
Every transaction affects at least two accounts and keeps Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity in balance
Accounts receivable is the money customers owe JKL for furniture already delivered on credit, the outstanding invoices
It is a short-term asset (due in less than one year) with a normal debit balance
It is really a line of credit the company extends to its customers, so it must be tracked and collected promptly
With more customers, JKL has more invoices to bill, follow up and collect
Accounts payable is money JKL owes its suppliers, shown on the liability side of the balance sheet
It is a short-term IOU to a creditor that must be paid within the agreed time to avoid default
The accounts payable job is to pay only bills that are legitimate and accurate, so the process must be very accurate
Verify each invoice against the purchase order and receiving record before paying

by_task.task: Concept of accounting and need for financial information
answer: Accounting is recording financial transactions, then storing, sorting, retrieving and summarizing the information into reports and analyses
Accounting provides the information needed to keep the business financially healthy
Managers use financial information to plan, control costs and make decisions; owners, banks and investors use it to judge performance; the government needs it for taxes
Accurate records matter because errors in a growing company multiply quickly: wrong bills get paid, customers are not collected from, and reports mislead decision makers

judge_question_answers.question: Why are ethics important in accounting?
answer: Owners, lenders, investors and the government rely on accounting reports being honest and accurate
Unethical accounting hides the true financial position and can lead to fraud, bad decisions and legal penalties
Ethical bookkeeping protects the company's money and reputation

judge_question_answers.question: How does the accounting department help to reinforce the company's image?
answer: Paying suppliers accurately and on time builds trust with vendors and keeps credit terms favorable
Accurate customer billing and professional collection practices show customers the company is reliable
Clean, timely financial statements give banks, investors and auditors confidence in the company

key_concepts.definition: Money a business owes its suppliers for purchases on credit; a short-term liability, an IOU that must be paid within the agreed time to avoid default.
Money customers owe the business for products or services already delivered on credit; a short-term asset with a normal debit balance.
Recording financial transactions and then storing, sorting, retrieving and summarizing them into reports and analyses that keep the business financially healthy.
Any exchange that changes the company's financial position and can be measured in money; each one affects at least two accounts.
A cash transaction is settled immediately; a credit (on account) transaction is settled later and creates an account receivable or account payable.
External transactions are exchanges with outside parties such as customers and suppliers; internal transactions, like using supplies or recording depreciation, happen within the company.
Managers (planning and control), owners and investors (performance), creditors (ability to repay) and government (taxes) all need accurate financial information.
Honesty, accuracy and objectivity in keeping records and preparing reports so that users can trust the financial information.

The president of the board of directors (judge) has asked for your help in developing an accounting plan to review and propose standard operating procedures around its finance functions.

SOCIETY FOR MARKETERS has existed for the past 40 years, but within the past five years has had to change its core mission, membership model, and programs and services offered to meet the changing needs of their professional members. solution.overview: A strong answer journalizes the cartridge sale as Accounts Receivable $25,000 to Sales and Cost of Goods Sold $15,000 to Inventory, but explains that under the revenue recognition principle the sale is not earned until the goods ship on 11/1, so it adds nothing to October net income. The $500 web hosting invoice is an October expense (matching principle) recorded as an expense and Accounts Payable, so it lowers October net income even though it is paid in November. It then explains that net-income bonuses encourage cost control but tempt managers to ship early or delay expenses, so controls and ethics matter.

answer: Transaction a: 500 cartridges x $50 = $25,000 of sales; debit Accounts Receivable 25,000, credit Sales 25,000
Transaction a also records the cost: 500 x $30 = $15,000; debit Cost of Goods Sold 15,000, credit Inventory 15,000
These entries are dated when the sale is earned, which is the shipping date 11/1, not 10/31
Transaction b: debit Web Hosting (or Marketing) Expense 500, credit Accounts Payable 500, recorded in October when the invoice is received
When the invoice is paid on November 15: debit Accounts Payable 500, credit Cash 500
Transaction a does not affect October net income because the cartridges were not shipped until November
The revenue recognition principle says revenue is recorded when earned; here it is earned when the goods ship, so the $25,000 sale and $15,000 cost belong to November
The $10,000 gross profit on the sale will raise November net income, and the manager's November bonus, instead
Transaction b: expenses are recorded when incurred, and the hosting fee is for October, so the $500 is an October expense even though it is paid November 15
Net income = revenue - expenses, so the $500 reduces October net income
The income statement reports revenue and expenses for a period, so timing decides which month each item belongs to
Basing bonuses on net income is better than basing them on revenue because it encourages managers to control costs too
But both methods create temptation to manipulate results: a manager might ship items before a real order exists to book revenue early
A manager might also push expenses into future periods to inflate the current month's net income
The controller must apply GAAP consistently (revenue recognition, matching) regardless of bonus pressure, and the company should have review controls and a clear bonus policy
Explaining the rules to the manager now prevents future disputes and protects the accuracy of the financial statements

answer: GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles): the principles, standards and procedures for financial accounting that improve consistency and comparability of financial reports

Other organizations: Accounting and Finance Women's Alliance, Institute of Management Accountants (IMA), National Association of Black Accountants, Institute of Internal Auditors, state CPA societies

Membership signals professionalism to employers and clients and keeps the accountant connected to changes in the field

key_concepts.definition: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles: the set of principles, standards and procedures that make financial statements consistent and comparable across companies.

American Institute of Certified Public Accountants: the national association of CPAs that sets ethical standards for the profession and develops the Uniform CPA Exam.
Certified Public Accountant: a licensed accountant who passed the CPA exam and met education and experience requirements; only CPAs can audit financial statements.

by_task.task: Describe the business trend and its risks

Examples: home sharing (Airbnb), car and ride sharing, parking space sharing, dog boarding, lending clubs, and now pool sharing apps

solution.overview: A strong answer explains that under accrual accounting revenue is recorded when earned (when produce is delivered to the grocery store) and expenses when incurred or when an asset is used, so profit for a period is measured correctly, which cash basis cannot do. It defines accounts receivable (asset, what customers owe, debit to increase) and accounts payable (liability, what the business owes vendors, credit to increase), then journalizes the three June transactions: Accounts Receivable/Sales $1,000, Refrigerator/Accounts Payable $2,000, Prepaid Insurance/Cash $3,000, and explains the follow-up entries.

by_task.task: How accrual accounting works and why it is preferred
answer: Accrual basis: revenue is recorded when earned, so when the fruits, vegetables and honey are delivered to the grocery store the sale is recognized even though cash has not arrived
Expenses are recorded when incurred or when an asset is used up, not when the bill is paid
This matches the expenses that were required to generate the revenue in the same period, so the owner can see the true profit for each month or year
Cash basis records only when cash moves, so revenue and the related expenses can land in different periods and profit for a period may be wrong
GAAP (accounting standards) requires accrual accounting, and larger customers, lenders and the IRS (once the business grows) expect it
Accounts receivable tracks how much all customers owe you, such as the grocery chain's $1,000 bill; it is an asset on the balance sheet
Accounts receivable increases with a debit and decreases with a credit when the customer pays
Accounts payable tracks how much you owe all vendors, such as the $2,000 refrigerator bill; it is a liability on the balance sheet
Accounts payable increases with a credit and decreases with a debit when you pay
Both accounts are used when buying and selling on trade credit
June 10: debit Accounts Receivable 1,000, credit Sales 1,000; revenue is recognized on delivery even though the store has not paid

Terms 2/10, n/30 mean the store may deduct 2% ($20) if it pays within 10 days, otherwise the full $1,000 is due in 30 days; if paid early, debit Cash 980 and Sales Discounts 20, credit Accounts Receivable 1,000
June 20: debit Refrigerator (Equipment) 2,000, credit Accounts Payable 2,000; the refrigerator is a long-term asset, not an expense, and the debt is recorded now even though payment is in July

June 30: debit Prepaid Insurance 3,000, credit Cash 3,000; the payment buys six months of coverage, so it is an asset that becomes expense at $500 per month (debit Insurance Expense 500, credit Prepaid Insurance 500 each month July through December)
Under cash basis the owner would have shown no June sale, no refrigerator debt and a $3,000 June expense, which distorts June's profit

journal_entries.description: June 10: sale of fruits, vegetables and honey to the grocery store on account, terms 2/10, n/30
June 20: purchase of a refrigerator on account, to be paid in July
June 30: prepaid liability insurance for the last six months of the year
Follow-up (model): monthly adjusting entry July through December to expense one month of insurance
Follow-up (model): grocery store pays within the 10-day discount period

calculations.result: $500 Insurance Expense per month, July through December

steps: 2% x 1,000 = 20 discount if paid within 10 days
calculations.result: $980 cash if paid by June 20; otherwise $1,000 due by July 10

judge_question_answers.question: How should expenses for bottling honey be classified?
answer: Bottling costs (jars, lids, labels, labor to fill them) are product costs: they become part of the inventory cost of the honey and are recorded as Cost of Goods Sold when the honey is sold
Under accrual accounting they are matched to the revenue from the honey sale, not expensed when the jars are bought
If the amounts are small, a simpler approach is a Packaging Supplies expense account, but keep it separate from selling and administrative expenses so gross profit on honey is visible

judge_question_answers.question: How can I tell if my business is doing well?
answer: Prepare an income statement each month under accrual accounting and check that net income (revenue minus expenses) is positive and growing
Watch the balance sheet: accounts receivable being collected on time, accounts payable paid on time and cash on hand to cover bills
Track ratios such as gross profit margin and net profit margin (net income / sales) and compare them month to month and to similar businesses
Compare actual results to a budget and to last year to spot trends

key_concepts.definition: Recording revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands; required by GAAP.
Recording revenue only when cash is received and expenses only when cash is paid; simple but can misstate profit for a period.
Revenue is recorded when earned, which for goods is when they are delivered to the customer, even if the customer has not paid.
Expenses are recorded in the same period as the revenue they helped produce so profit for the period is measured correctly.
An asset account tracking what customers owe the business; increases with a debit, decreases with a credit when collected.
A liability account tracking what the business owes its vendors; increases with a credit, decreases with a debit when paid.
The buyer may take a 2% discount if it pays within 10 days; otherwise the full amount is due within 30 days.
A payment made in advance for a future benefit, such as six months of insurance; recorded as an asset and moved to expense as it is used (3,000 / 6 = 500 per month).
An end-of-period entry that updates accounts under accrual accounting, such as expensing one month of prepaid insurance.
A long-lived item like a refrigerator that is recorded as an asset when bought and depreciated over its useful life, rather than expensed.
The balance sheet lists assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time (accounts receivable and payable live here); the income statement shows revenue, expenses and net income for a period.
Generally Accepted Accounting Principles: the standards that require accrual accounting so financial statements are consistent and comparable.

answer: The intern's first entry says 'to close revenue' but actually credited Cash, an asset, for $145,000
Cash is a permanent (real) account and is never closed, so the entry must be reversed
Correction: debit Cash $145,000, credit Owner's Capital $145,000
This restores the $145,000 cash balance to the books and removes the wrong debit from capital
Revenue is a temporary (nominal) account and must be closed at year end; the intern never closed it
The company does not use Income Summary, so revenue closes straight to Owner's Capital
Closing entry: debit Revenue $1,112,432, credit Owner's Capital $1,112,432
After this entry Revenue has a zero balance and is ready to collect next year's lessons revenue
Debits: Cash 145,000; Prepaid Insurance 4,332; Supplies 2,213; Furniture 4,321; Equipment 24,321 = 180,187
Credits: Accounts Payable 1,511; Owner's Capital 178,676 = 180,187
Owner's Capital moves from a 1,078,756 debit (impossible for a healthy business) to a 178,676 credit
Only permanent accounts (assets, liabilities, equity) appear; Revenue is gone because it is closed

by_task.task: Discuss the intern's errors and the corrections
answer: Error 1: the intern treated Cash as if it were revenue and closed it; permanent accounts carry their balances into the next year
Error 2: the actual Revenue account, a temporary account, was left open; temporary accounts (revenue, expenses, withdrawals) must be closed to capital
The tell-tale sign was a huge debit balance in Owner's Capital and a revenue account still on a post-closing trial balance
Accounting equation check: Assets 180,187 = Liabilities 1,511 + Owner's Equity 178,676
Accurate closing matters because the owner is deciding whether to open a fourth studio and needs reliable financial information

judge_question_answers.question: Explain why the owner should or should not open another studio location?
answer: The corrected numbers show the business is profitable: net income of about $155,032 on $1.1 million of revenue, with $145,000 cash on hand and only $1,511 of payables
Five years in business and three full studios suggest steady demand, which supports expansion
Before committing, the owner should confirm the new location's projected revenue covers the added rent, staff and setup costs, and check whether the $145,000 cash is enough or financing is needed
Recommend opening only if a break-even analysis for the new studio shows a reasonable payback period

judge_question_answers.question: What overhead and operating costs should be considered in opening another studio location?
answer: Operating costs: instructor and receptionist wages, payroll taxes, manager salary, cleaning, supplies, credit card fees
Overhead: rent for the new space, utilities, internet, insurance, repairs and maintenance, advertising for the launch
One-time start-up costs: furniture, registration laptops and equipment (which then create depreciation expense each year)
Use the current studios' expense pattern (for example, rent of $72,000 for three studios, about $24,000 each) to estimate the fourth studio

key_concepts.definition: Year-end journal entries that transfer the balances of temporary accounts (revenues, expenses, withdrawals) to the owner's capital account so they start the new period at zero.
Asset, liability and owner's capital accounts whose balances carry forward to the next accounting period. They are never closed.
Revenue, expense and withdrawal accounts that track one period's activity and are closed to capital at year end.
A list of all accounts with balances after closing entries are posted. It contains only permanent accounts and proves total debits equal total credits.
An optional temporary account used to collect revenues and expenses during closing before the net amount is moved to capital. Dance Frenzy skips it and closes directly to Owner's Capital.
A journal entry that fixes an earlier mistake, often by reversing the wrong entry (debit what was wrongly credited and vice versa) and then recording the right one.
Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity. Every transaction and every closing entry must keep the equation in balance.
Revenue minus expenses for the period. Net income increases owner's capital; withdrawals decrease it.
Cash or other assets the owner takes out of the business for personal use, a temporary account closed to capital at year end.

Overhead covers ongoing costs of running the business such as rent, utilities, insurance and administration; operating costs are the direct costs of delivering the service such as instructor wages and supplies.
Owners and managers rely on accurate statements to make decisions such as expanding to a new location, so errors in closing can lead to poor decisions.

roleplays.title: Sneaker reseller (NOOK Dunk Low): FIFO cost of goods sold and gross profit, and comparing the four inventory valuation methods
roleplays.participant_role: Entrepreneur and accounting student who runs a sneaker resale business and has calculated cost of goods sold on the NOOK Dunk Low
roleplays.judge_role: Tax accountant meeting the entrepreneur to review cost of goods sold and inventory valuation methods
roleplays.scenario:
You are to assume the role of an entrepreneur that is also an accounting student. Your tax accountant (judge) will be meeting with you to discuss your cost of goods sold and inventory valuation methods.

You have started your own business as a sneaker reseller who buys sneakers and attempts to sell them for a profit. You are getting ready to meet with your tax accountant (judge) to discuss the cost of goods sold. Since you have been studying accounting, you have decided to calculate this yourself. You are familiar with the four methods of valuing inventory: specific identification, First-in, First-out (FIFO), Last-in, First-out (LIFO) and weighted averages.

You have decided to do the calculation on only the transactions related to the popular NOOK brand Dunk Low sneaker. You want to verify understanding of the process with the tax accountant (judge).

The NOOK Dunk Low sneaker was launched on the NOOK SNKRS app in early June. There was immense hype with sneaker fans for this product launch. Therefore, you felt that the shoe would quickly increase in value and be a profitable investment.

You will use the following transactions to calculate cost of goods sold and gross profit using FIFO:

June 3rd: You win the draw for the shoe on the NOOK SNKRS app and purchase it for retail at $100.
June 5th: A friend also wins the draw on the NOOK SNKRS app and you buy their pair for $180.
June 7th: You purchase four pairs of the shoe from SNEAKER KICKS CO. for $210 each.
June 13th: You purchase 2 more pairs of the shoe from another reseller at SNEAKERCON for $250 each.
June 21st: You sell 3 pairs of the shoe for $270 each.

You will meet with the tax accountant (judge) to discuss the following:
- Review the calculations
- Verify understanding of the four inventory valuation methods
- Explain which method will generate the lowest gross profit based on the transactions above in which the costs are rising

You will present the information to the tax accountant (judge) in a role-play to take place in the tax accountant's (judge's) office. The tax accountant (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the tax accountant's (judge's) questions, the tax accountant (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

solution.overview: A strong answer walks through FIFO: the 3 pairs sold on June 21 are costed at the three oldest purchases ($100 + $180 + $210 = $490), so gross profit is $810 minus $490 = $320 and the remaining 5 pairs (3 at $210 and 2 at $250, $1,130) stay in inventory. The presenter then defines specific identification, FIFO, LIFO and weighted average, and concludes that with rising costs LIFO gives the lowest gross profit ($100 here) because the newest, most expensive pairs go into cost of goods sold.

by_task.task: FIFO cost of goods sold and gross profit
answer: 8 pairs were bought for a total of $1,620 (100 + 180 + 840 + 500)
FIFO sells the oldest pairs first: June 3 pair $100, June 5 pair $180, one June 7 pair $210
Cost of goods sold = $100 + $180 + $210 = $490
Sales = 3 x $270 = $810; gross profit = $810 minus $490 = $320
Ending inventory = 3 pairs at $210 + 2 pairs at $250 = $1,130 (check: $1,620 minus $490)
Specific identification: used for high-cost, low-volume items; COGS is the actual cost of the exact pairs sold (workable for sneakers if each pair is tracked by receipt)
FIFO: the most used method; COGS uses the older purchases and ending inventory is made up of the newer purchases
LIFO: COGS uses the newest purchases and ending inventory is made up of the older purchases
Weighted average: one average cost per unit ($1,620 / 8 = $202.50) is used for both COGS and ending inventory
All four are cost-flow assumptions; the physical pair handed to the buyer can be any of them (except under specific identification)

by_task.task: Which method gives the lowest gross profit when costs are rising
answer: LIFO, because the most recent (highest) purchase costs make up cost of goods sold
LIFO here: 2 x $250 + 1 x $210 = $710 COGS, gross profit $810 minus $710 = $100
Compare: FIFO gross profit $320, weighted average $202.50 (COGS 3 x $202.50 = $607.50), LIFO $100
Lower gross profit means lower taxable income, which is why a tax accountant cares about the method choice
Whatever method is chosen must be used consistently from year to year

June 21 cost of the 3 pairs sold under FIFO

calculations.label: Cost of goods available for sale
LIFO and weighted average comparison (model answer, not in PDF)
steps: LIFO COGS: 2 x $250 + 1 x $210 = $710; gross profit $810 minus $710 = $100
Weighted average cost: $1,620 / 8 = $202.50; COGS 3 x $202.50 = $607.50; gross profit $810 minus $607.50 = $202.50
calculations.result: Gross profit: FIFO $320 > weighted average $202.50 > LIFO $100

judge_question_answers.question: Why is it important to calculate cost of goods sold?
answer: COGS is subtracted from sales to find gross profit, the first measure of whether the resale business actually makes money
It determines taxable income, so it must be calculated correctly and consistently for the tax return
It shows the true profit per pair, which guides what price to pay for future sneakers and what price to sell at
It also sets the value of ending inventory reported on the balance sheet

judge_question_answers.question: When is it appropriate to use Last in First out (LIFO)?
answer: When costs are rising and the business wants to match current (higher) costs against current sales, which lowers reported profit and taxes
For goods that are not perishable and where the physical flow does not matter, such as bulk materials or, here, identical sneakers
Only where it is allowed: US GAAP and the IRS permit LIFO (with a conformity rule that it be used for both books and taxes), but IFRS does not
Not appropriate when costs are falling, when inventory turns over very quickly, or when the physical flow is clearly first-in first-out

key_concepts.definition: The cost of the inventory actually sold during the period. Under a cost-flow method, COGS = Units sold x Cost assigned to those units.
Sales revenue minus cost of goods sold; the profit before operating expenses and taxes.
Assumes the oldest costs are sold first, so COGS is made of older purchases and ending inventory of newer purchases. In rising-cost periods it gives the highest gross profit.
Assumes the newest costs are sold first, so COGS is made of the most recent purchases. In rising-cost periods it gives the lowest gross profit and lowest taxes.
Assigns every unit the same average cost: Total cost of goods available / Total units available. Here $1,620 / 8 = $202.50 per pair.
Tracks the actual cost of each individual item sold; practical for high-cost, low-volume goods like cars, jewelry or collectible sneakers.

key_concepts.term: Cost of goods available for sale
key_concepts.definition: Beginning inventory + Purchases during the period; it is split between COGS and ending inventory.
Cost of goods available minus COGS; the value of unsold units carried on the balance sheet as a current asset.
An accounting choice about which costs are assigned to sold units; it does not have to match which physical pair the customer received.
A business should apply the same inventory method every period so results are comparable; a change must be justified and disclosed.
US tax rule that a business using LIFO for its tax return must also use LIFO in its financial statements.

solution.overview: A strong answer defines internal users (people inside the company making managerial decisions) and external users (outsiders such as banks, suppliers and auditors making investing and credit decisions), explains that GAAP is the common set of rules set by the FASB so outsiders can trust and compare financial statements, and then classifies each of the six users, using plain, non-technical language for a small-business owner.

answer: External users do not work for the company; they use the financial statements to make decisions such as investing or giving credit
Internal users work for the company and use the information for managerial decision making (pricing, staffing, expansion)
Internal users can see detailed reports (quantities sold, salaries); external users generally see only the GAAP financial statements
Because outsiders rely on the statements, the records cannot be a private system only the owner understands

by_task.task: Explain why the company must use GAAP
answer: GAAP is a common set of standards (rules) set by the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB)
The rules let external users compare the performance of different companies on the same basis
Banks and suppliers usually require GAAP statements before lending or extending credit
An external auditor can only give an opinion if the statements follow a recognized standard like GAAP
Owner: internal, works for the company, sees internal reports (quantities sold, salaries) and uses them for strategy and operating efficiency
Bank: external, uses GAAP financial statements to assess creditworthiness before lending
External Auditor: external, independent of the company, examines the financial information and expresses an opinion on its accuracy
Suppliers: external, check that the company is a going concern that can pay its bills, protecting the supplier's future sales
Internal Auditor: internal, works for the company and tests internal controls
Marketing Manager: internal, uses financial information for forecasting decisions

judge_question_answers.question: How can improper accounting affect customers?
answer: Wrong cost and profit figures can lead to bad pricing decisions, so customers may be overcharged or the shop may run short on cash and cut quality or service
If the shop cannot pay suppliers or lenders because its books were misleading, it may close and customers lose the business
Customer records (gift cards, loyalty credits, refunds) may be mishandled if bookkeeping is unreliable

judge_question_answers.question: How can improper accounting lead to illegal activity?
answer: Misstated revenue or expenses can mean under-reported income and unpaid taxes (tax evasion)
False financial statements given to a bank to get a loan is fraud
Weak records and controls make it easy to hide theft or embezzlement by employees or owners

key_concepts.definition: The common set of accounting rules and standards US companies follow so that financial statements are consistent, reliable and comparable.
The private organization that sets GAAP in the United States.
People inside the company (owner, managers, internal auditor) who use detailed accounting information to run the business and make managerial decisions.
People outside the company (banks, suppliers, investors, external auditors, government) who rely on the financial statements to make investing, lending and credit decisions.
An examination of a company's financial statements by an independent outside accountant who gives an opinion on whether they are fairly presented under GAAP.
A review done by employees of the company to test internal controls, catch errors and fraud, and improve operations; it reports to management rather than to outsiders.
Procedures such as separating duties, approvals and reconciliations that protect assets and keep the accounting records accurate.
The assumption that a business will keep operating and paying its debts for the foreseeable future; suppliers and lenders check for this.
A lender's judgment of how likely a borrower is to repay, based largely on GAAP financial statements.
The financial statements (income statement, balance sheet, cash flow statement) a company gives to outside parties, prepared under GAAP.
Explaining accounting ideas in plain language and examples that fit the listener, here a small-business owner without an accounting background.

by_task.task: Classify each account and its statement
answer: Dumbbells and Treadmills (Equipment): asset, balance sheet
Personal trainers' salaries (Salaries Expense): expense, income statement
Cash in the gym's bank account (Cash): asset, balance sheet
Bills that the gym must pay (Accounts Payable): liability, balance sheet
Invoices that current members owe the gym (Accounts Receivable): asset, balance sheet
Owner's capital: equity, balance sheet (also shown on the statement of owner's equity)
Number the accounts by type: 100s assets, 200s liabilities, 300s equity, 400s revenue, 500s expenses
Example: 110 Cash, 120 Accounts Receivable, 150 Equipment, 210 Accounts Payable, 310 Owner's Capital, 410 Membership Revenue, 510 Salaries Expense
Accounts receivable is money members owe for invoices already sent; it is an asset because the gym expects to collect it
Leave gaps in the numbering so new accounts (Insurance Expense, Supplies) can be added later

by_task.task: Purpose of the three financial statements
answer: Income Statement: shows revenue, expenses and profit over a period of time; the bottom line is net income or net loss (revenue less expenses)
Statement of Owner's Equity: shows changes in the owner's financial interest over a period; beginning capital plus net income less withdrawals equals ending capital
Balance Sheet: shows the balances of assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time and represents the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity)
The statements link: net income flows into the statement of owner's equity, and ending capital flows into the balance sheet

judge_question_answers.question: What types of insurance do we need?
answer: General liability insurance in case a member is injured on the equipment or in a class
Property insurance covering the building contents and equipment (treadmills, ellipticals, weights)
Workers' compensation for the trainers and staff, and professional liability for the personal trainers
Business interruption insurance to cover lost membership income if the gym must close temporarily

judge_question_answers.question: Where does insurance fit into the accounts?
answer: Insurance paid in advance is recorded as Prepaid Insurance, an asset on the balance sheet
As each month of coverage is used up, the cost moves to Insurance Expense on the income statement (an adjusting entry)
Any premium owed but not yet paid is a liability (Accounts Payable or Insurance Payable)

key_concepts.definition: The numbered list of every account a business uses, grouped as assets, liabilities, equity, revenue and expenses.
Something the business owns or is owed that has future value, such as cash, equipment and accounts receivable.
A debt or obligation the business owes to others, such as accounts payable (bills to be paid).
The owner's financial interest in the business: what is left after liabilities are subtracted from assets.
Revenue is money earned from providing services (memberships, training); expenses are the costs of running the business (salaries, rent). Revenue less expenses equals net income.
Amounts customers owe the business for services already provided and invoiced; an asset expected to be collected soon.
Bills the business owes to suppliers and others for goods or services already received; a current liability.
Reports revenue, expenses and net income or net loss over a period of time (a month, quarter or year).
Shows how the owner's capital changed over a period: beginning capital + net income (or minus net loss) minus withdrawals = ending capital.
Shows assets, liabilities and owner's equity at a single point in time and proves the accounting equation.
Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity; every transaction keeps this equation in balance.
Insurance paid in advance; recorded as an asset and then expensed month by month as the coverage is used.

answer: Goods available: 5 x $46 = $230; 20 x $39 = $780; 8 x $43 = $344; total 33 units costing $1,354
Weighted average cost = $1,354 / 33 = $41.03 per pound
COGS = 12 units sold x $41.03 = $492.36
Ending inventory = 21 units x $41.03 = about $861.64 (total cost 1,354 minus 492.36)
Gross profit = $612.00 minus COGS $492.36 = $119.64
Gross margin = 119.64 / 612 = about 19.5%
Journal entries under a perpetual system: debit Cash or A/R 612, credit Sales 612; debit COGS 492.36, credit Inventory 492.36
Weighted average is good at smoothing out large swings in cost, like the $39 to $46 range here
Crab legs spoil, so the real physical flow is first-in first-out: sell the oldest pounds first to avoid losses
If the owner wants recorded COGS to follow the actual flow of the product, switch to FIFO
FIFO also leaves ending inventory on the balance sheet at the most recent prices rather than older ones
ASC 330-10-30-9 says to pick the method that most clearly reflects periodic income; for a perishable seller that points to FIFO
Comparison for October: FIFO COGS = 5 x 46 + 7 x 39 = $503 (gross profit $109); LIFO COGS = 8 x 43 + 4 x 39 = $500 (gross profit $112); weighted average $492.36 (gross profit $119.64)

judge_question_answers.question: How does product spoilage affect inventory?
answer: Spoiled product can no longer be sold, so it must be written off: debit a Spoilage or Inventory Loss expense, credit Inventory
It lowers the ending inventory value and raises expenses, cutting gross profit
Spoilage risk is why perishable sellers physically rotate stock first-in first-out and keep inventory levels low
Regular physical counts catch spoilage so the books match what is actually in the case

judge_question_answers.question: In a seafood market, should all perishable products use the same inventory method?

solution.overview: A strong answer walks the owner through the eight steps of the accounting cycle, labels the four transactions as a sale, a purchase, a cash receipt and a cash payment, then shows each one on the accounting equation: assets rise by $100,000 (receivable), $36,000 (inventory) and $50,000 (cash) and fall by $23,500 (cash), while liabilities rise $36,000 and equity rises $150,000 of revenue less $23,500 of wages expense. answer: 1. Identify transactions from source documents (invoices, receipts, payroll records)
2. Record transactions in the journal (journalize)
3. Post the journal entries to the general ledger accounts
4. Prepare an unadjusted trial balance
5. Analyze a worksheet and 6. record adjusting entries (accruals, depreciation, supplies used)
7. Generate the financial statements, then 8. close the temporary accounts (revenue, expenses, drawings) to start the next period
Sale of 10,000 bags for $100,000 on account: a sales (credit sale) transaction; revenue earned now, cash collected later
Purchase of 4,000 pounds of beans for $36,000 on account: a purchase transaction; inventory acquired, owed to the vendor
Customer pays $50,000 for 5,000 bags: a receipt (cash sale) transaction; cash and revenue at the same time
Wages of $23,500 paid: a payment (cash disbursement) transaction for an expense
Sale on account: Accounts Receivable (asset) up $100,000; Sales Revenue raises equity $100,000
Purchase on account: Inventory (asset) up $36,000; Accounts Payable (liability) up $36,000; equity unchanged
Cash sale: Cash (asset) up $50,000; Sales Revenue raises equity $50,000
Wages paid: Cash (asset) down $23,500; Salaries and Wage Expense lowers equity $23,500
Every transaction changes at least two items and the equation stays balanced after each one
Liabilities: +$36,000

It shows who has claims on the assets: creditors (liabilities) and the owner (equity)

Selling goods with payment due later; increases Accounts Receivable and Sales Revenue.
Buying goods or inventory with payment due later; increases Inventory and Accounts Payable.
Receiving cash, such as a cash sale or a customer paying an invoice; increases Cash.
Paying cash out for expenses or bills, such as wages; decreases Cash and either records an expense or reduces a liability.
Money customers owe for sales made on credit; an asset.
Money the business owes vendors for purchases made on credit; a liability.
Goods held for sale, such as coffee beans; an asset until sold, when its cost becomes cost of goods sold.
Revenue increases owner's equity and expenses decrease it; net income = revenue - expenses flows into equity.
A list of all ledger accounts and balances used to check that total debits equal total credits before statements are prepared.
Transferring revenue, expense and drawing balances to owner's capital so they start the next period at zero.

2. Debit Cash $420, credit Sales Revenue (toys) $420
4. Debit Cash $75, credit Sales Revenue (supplies) $75

The $150 for display racks is a one-time cost, so net cash should be higher in future weeks; advertising may also be infrequent
The $200 food restock was about the same as the $183 of food sales; without gross margin data it is hard to judge, and the store may run short of food choices in coming weeks
